blocks.text: FSDP, fully sharded data parallel, extends the data parallelism idea covered earlier in this module by additionally sharding, splitting, the model parameters themselves across devices, rather than requiring every device to hold a complete model copy, gathering the full parameters only briefly when actually needed for computation.

This topic explains how FSDP combines the simplicity of data parallelism with meaningful memory savings, setting up a direct comparison with the ZeRO stages covered later in this module, which share a very similar underlying idea.
1. What FSDP Stands For

blocks.alt: Fully Sharded Data Parallel gives FSDP its name

blocks.text: FSDP stands for Fully Sharded Data Parallel, a name that directly describes its core idea, it is fundamentally a data parallel technique, splitting the batch across devices the way covered in the earlier Data Parallelism topic, but with the model parameters themselves also fully sharded rather than fully replicated.
2. The Problem FSDP Solves

blocks.alt: Standard data parallelism needs a full model copy per device while FSDP shards the model across devices

blocks.text: Standard data parallelism, covered earlier, requires every device to hold a full model copy, which limits its usefulness for very large models. FSDP removes this requirement by splitting the parameters themselves across the participating devices, so no single device needs to hold the entire model at once.
3. Sharding Parameters Across Devices

Under FSDP, each device permanently holds only a fraction, a shard, of the total model parameters, rather than the full set, meaning the total model memory footprint gets divided across all participating devices instead of duplicated on each one.
4. Gathering Parameters Just in Time

blocks.alt: A layer needing full parameters gathers them from all devices, computes, then discards them

blocks.text: When a specific layer computation actually needs its full parameters, FSDP temporarily gathers the relevant shards from across all devices, uses them briefly for that computation, and then discards the gathered full copy again, keeping only the permanent shard, a just in time approach that trades some communication for substantial permanent memory savings.

code.content:
# A conceptual sketch of the FSDP gather-compute-discard pattern
for layer in model.layers:
    full_params = gather_shards_from_all_devices(layer.local_shard)
    output = layer.forward(input_data, full_params)
    discard(full_params)  # only the local shard is kept permanently

blocks.text: 5. FSDP vs Standard Data Parallelism

blocks.alt: Standard data parallelism is compared against FSDP

blocks.text: Standard data parallelism trades simplicity for higher per device memory usage, every device holds everything, while FSDP trades some added complexity and communication for dramatically lower per device memory usage, letting significantly larger models be trained across the same number of devices.

blocks.text: 6. FSDP and Memory Savings

blocks.alt: Per-device memory gets sharply reduced with FSDP

blocks.text: The memory savings from FSDP scale directly with the number of participating devices, more devices means each one holds a smaller shard, making FSDP an increasingly powerful tool for fitting very large models as more hardware becomes available, unlike standard data parallelism where per device memory usage stays fixed regardless of device count.

blocks.title: This connects directly to the VRAM Management topic
blocks.content: FSDP specifically targets model weight memory, one of the four VRAM consumers covered in the earlier VRAM Management topic, spreading that specific cost across devices rather than duplicating it.

blocks.text: 7. FSDP's Communication Pattern

blocks.alt: Gather parameters, compute the layer, then re-shard parameters

blocks.text: FSDP communication happens repeatedly throughout training, gathering shards before each layer computation and effectively re-sharding, discarding the gathered copy, afterward, a real overhead cost that is generally well worth the substantial memory savings it enables.
8. FSDP in Modern Fine-Tuning Frameworks

FSDP has become a standard, well supported feature across many modern fine-tuning frameworks, covered further in the Fine-Tuning Frameworks module later in this course, making it accessible to configure without needing to implement its sharding and gathering logic manually.
9. When FSDP Is the Right Choice

FSDP is the right choice specifically when a model is too large for standard data parallelism, every device holding a full copy, but the team still wants the relative simplicity of a data parallel style training loop rather than manually designing a custom model or pipeline parallelism split.
Worked Example

A team with four GPUs wants to fine-tune a model too large for any single device to hold a full copy of, ruling out standard data parallelism. Rather than manually splitting the model with the layer level or tensor parallelism techniques covered earlier in this module, they use FSDP.

Each of their four devices permanently holds only a quarter of the total model parameters, gathering full layer parameters temporarily as needed during the forward and backward pass, successfully training a model that would never have fit under standard data parallelism, with meaningfully less manual implementation effort than a custom parallelism split would have required.
Common Mistakes

items: Choosing standard data parallelism for a model too large to fit as a full copy on each device, when FSDP would solve the problem directly
Underestimating FSDP's communication overhead from repeatedly gathering and discarding full parameters
Assuming FSDP eliminates the need for any other memory saving technique, rather than combining it with quantization or PEFT where appropriate
Not recognizing FSDP as fundamentally still a data parallel approach, just with sharded rather than replicated parameters

blocks.text: Practice

For a model size and a number of available devices you choose, estimate how much per-device memory FSDP would need for the model parameters alone, compared against what standard data parallelism, requiring a full copy per device, would need instead.
Key Takeaway

FSDP extends data parallelism by sharding the model parameters across devices rather than replicating them fully, gathering the full parameters only temporarily when a specific computation needs them, letting significantly larger models be trained with the relative simplicity of a data parallel training loop, at the cost of repeated inter-device communication for the gathering and re-sharding process.
